opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The core reason is that what we actually care about, especially from a risk perspective, is whether a model can *do things in the world*, not whether it has some isolated capability in the abstract. If you're asking "could this system autonomously replicate, or meaningfully accelerate AI research, or carry out a cyberattack end to end," those are long, messy tasks. They involve chaining together many steps, recovering from mistakes, dealing with ambiguous instructions, figuring out what information you're missing, and deciding when something is actually done.

Skill-isolating benchmarks are useful, but they have a couple of problems. First, the mapping from "scores well on this component skill" to "can do the whole task" is really unclear. You can have a model that looks great on every individual sub-skill and still falls apart over a multi-hour task, because the bottleneck turns out to be something you didn't think to measure, like noticing it's going in circles, or keeping track of state over a long horizon. And the reverse happens too: models sometimes find routes to completing a task that don't go through the skills you assumed were necessary.

Second, narrow benchmarks saturate fast and are easy to overfit to, whether deliberately or just through the general pressure of everyone optimizing against them. So you get these numbers that go up and it's hard to know what they mean for actual capability.

With whole tasks, the output is much more interpretable. Saying "the model can reliably complete tasks that take a skilled human professional about an hour, and that horizon has been doubling on a fairly regular schedule" is something a policymaker or a lab can actually reason about. It connects directly to the question of what these systems could do if deployed, or if they were trying to do something we didn't want.

It's definitely more expensive. You need realistic environments, human baselines to calibrate difficulty, careful scoring, and you have to think about elicitation, making sure you're getting the model's real best effort rather than underestimating it because of a bad scaffold. But if the goal is to avoid being surprised by dangerous capabilities, I think measuring the thing you actually care about, as directly as you can, is worth that cost.

r001.rationale: The response says skill-isolating benchmarks have unclear links to whole-task ability and that narrow benchmarks saturate and are easy to overfit, communicating the stated concern.

r002.rationale: It favors measuring success on long real-world tasks, but does not say those tasks are excluded from training or argue that success on diverse, challenging tasks implies possession of the capabilities needed to complete them.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that the thing we actually care about isn't any individual skill. It's whether a model can go out and do something in the world that matters, and specifically whether it could do something dangerous. When I'm trying to answer the question "could this system autonomously replicate, or meaningfully accelerate a bioweapons program, or carry out a cyberattack end to end," a benchmark that measures, say, code completion accuracy in isolation just doesn't tell me that.

The problem with isolated-skill benchmarks is that real tasks are mostly about the glue. It's about noticing that your first approach didn't work, figuring out why, recovering from an error you made three steps ago, deciding what to do when the instructions are ambiguous, managing a long context where you've accumulated a bunch of state. Models can be very good at the individual components and still fall apart completely when you chain them together over hours. Or sometimes the opposite happens, where a model looks mediocre on some narrow benchmark but is actually quite capable of muddling through a real task because it keeps trying things. You just can't predict the whole from the parts very well right now, and that's exactly the regime where I don't want to be guessing.

There's also a contamination and Goodhart issue. The moment a benchmark becomes well known, it ends up in training data, or labs tune toward it, and the number stops meaning what it used to mean. Messy, realistic tasks are harder to game because there isn't a single clean answer to memorize, and the space of plausible tasks is enormous.

And then there's the question of who the audience is. If I go to a policymaker or a lab and say the model got 73 percent on some abstract reasoning suite, nobody knows what to do with that. If I say, this model was given a laptop and a cloud account and completed tasks that take a human researcher a full day, and here's what it did and where it failed, that's legible. People can look at the transcript and form their own judgment about how worried to be.

Now, I don't want to oversell it. Realistic tasks are expensive to build, hard to score, and noisy, and you can't run thousands of them. So we do use narrower things as cheap early warning signals. But I treat those as proxies that need to be validated against the real thing, not as the ground truth. The ground truth is: can it do the job.

r001.rationale: The response says known benchmarks can enter training data or prompt labs to tune toward them, causing scores to lose meaning; it also discusses isolated-skill benchmarks.

r002.rationale: The response treats real-task performance as the ground truth and discusses long tasks, but does not clearly state that success on diverse, challenging tasks excluded from training implies the model has the capabilities needed to complete them.

astra-6.text:
I think the thing we ultimately care about is whether an AI can actually accomplish something useful in the world. A benchmark that isolates a particular skill can help you understand the system, but there’s a gap between demonstrating that skill and being able to use it reliably as part of a larger task.

For example, a model might be very good at answering a well-specified coding question, but doing an actual software engineering task also requires understanding what’s needed, navigating a codebase, testing your changes, and noticing when your approach isn’t working. You can be excellent at individual pieces and still fail to put them together.

And it can go the other way: a system might do poorly on a particular benchmark but accomplish the real task using tools or a different approach. So I’d like evaluations to preserve that freedom while measuring whether the outcome was actually achieved. That gives us a more direct handle on what people could use these systems for, including potentially dangerous things.

r001.rationale: The response describes a gap between isolated-skill benchmarks and useful performance, but does not identify a tendency to overfit those benchmarks.

r002.rationale: The response favors measuring real-world outcomes, but does not say that success on diverse, challenging tasks excluded from training implies the system has the capabilities to complete them.

sol-6.1.text:
Because what we ultimately care about is whether an AI can actually get something useful done. A benchmark that isolates one skill can tell you something about that skill, but there can be a big gap between that and completing a task. The system might be very good at writing individual pieces of code, for example, but struggle to work out what needs changing, test its solution, or recover when something goes wrong.

With an end-to-end task, you’re testing whether all those capabilities fit together. Can it sustain progress, notice mistakes, and produce a result that meets the actual requirements? Those things can be bottlenecks even when the individual skills look impressive.

I think isolated benchmarks are still useful for diagnosing why a system fails. But if you want to understand its practical capabilities—and the risks associated with those capabilities—you need to measure how well it can accomplish realistic goals.

r001.rationale: The response says isolated benchmarks may not predict task completion, but it does not identify a tendency to overfit those benchmarks.

r002.rationale: It favors testing realistic end-to-end tasks, but does not claim that success on diverse, challenging, long tasks excluded from training implies the needed capabilities.
